title: Who speaks of my brother?
hookLine: a hungry old vulture hears his brother's name
carry: tarpana: water poured, a loved one named

lines: AN OLD BIRD ON THE ROCKS.
cards: Out of a cave on the hillside comes an enormous old bird. What's left of his wings is burned. He drags himself onto the rocks and looks down at a beach covered with monkeys, all sitting perfectly still.
And he says to himself, more or less: what luck. A meal, lined up and waiting to die. As each one goes, I'll eat him.
The monkeys hear him. Nobody on that beach is sitting quite so still anymore.

teach.b: The monkeys are terrified. Angada, already in despair, says it aloud: death has come for us in the shape of a bird. Even Jatayu gave his life for Rama, he says.
We're dying for Rama too. The old bird freezes. Who is speaking of my brother? he calls down.
I haven't heard that name in so long. Is Jatayu dead? The hunter has become a mourner.
His name is Sampati, and Jatayu was his younger brother. The monkeys, still uneasy, help him down, and Angada tells him everything: Sita taken, Jatayu's fight with Ravana in the sky, and his death.
Sampati grieves right there on the beach.

teach.h: TARPANA: WATER POURED, A LOVED ONE NAMED.
teach.b: And in Valmiki's telling, he asks the monkeys to carry him to the edge of the sea, so he can offer water to his brother. They carry him down, and the old bird pours water for Jatayu.
This is one of the oldest things Hindus do for their dead. It's called tarpana.
You pour water from cupped hands, often with sesame seeds in it, and you say the person's name, and the names of your parents and grandparents before them.
Families do it in the shraddha rites after a death, and every year in Pitru Paksha, the fortnight for the ancestors. The teaching under it: the people we lose aren't simply gone.
They're named, fed and remembered, and the bond keeps running. Jatayu's death looked like a defeat months ago in the story. Now his name, said out loud on a beach, saves the whole southern party.

how: Tarpana is offered in the shraddha rites after a death and every year in Pitru Paksha, often with sesame seeds in the water, naming the departed and, commonly, three generations of ancestors. Storytellers often pair Sampati and Jatayu as two brothers who both serve Rama.

o: the vulture king who fought Ravana in the sky
Jatayu's elder brother, the old vulture with burned wings
a rakshasa who guards the southern shore of the sea

games.q: the bird on the hill — tap the pairs.
p: water offered with a loved one's name

s: Sampati asks to be carried to the sea to offer water for Jatayu
that water offering, tarpana, is still how Hindus honor their dead.
hearing Jatayu's name changes Sampati's whole manner
he calls down asking who speaks of his brother.
Sampati already knew Jatayu had died
he learns it from the monkeys and grieves.

games.q: you're Sampati, old and hungry, looking at a line of monkeys who've sat down to die. then you hear your brother's name. what do you do?
o: call down and ask who is speaking of your brother.
games.why: Sampati asks about Jatayu, and the monkeys help him down and tell him the whole story.

practice: Think of someone you've lost, a grandparent, a friend, anyone, and say their name silently, or aloud if you're alone.
Cup your hands, with a little water in them if you have some, and as you breathe out, let it go, the way Sampati did for his brother. Breathe in and let the name stay warm in your chest.
If no one comes to mind, think of someone who carries a loss, and hold them instead.

wordCard.voice: Sampati. The wingless old vulture who comes for a meal, hears his brother's name, and becomes family.

orig.note: Sanskrit sampāti: the elder brother of Jatayu, a great vulture.

carryVoice: Your line: tarpana, water poured, a loved one named. Tomorrow, how Sampati lost his wings. Day five hundred ninety-nine, done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 56–58 (Sampati appears; Angada's lament; Sampati asks about Jatayu and offers water for him)
